title: About the CC exam
description: What the CC exam looks like, how its adaptive format works, how to read and pace its questions, and the steps around it, from booking to staying certified. Written in plain language by KaiSip from ISC2's published information.
disclaimer: KaiSip is an independent study app. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by ISC2. ISC2® and CC® are registered trademarks of ISC2, Inc., used here only to describe the exam. ISC2 alone sets the exam rules and decides certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: The facts on this page were checked on the date shown. Exam rules can change, so check isc2.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: A computer-based exam of 100 to 125 questions in up to 2 hours. It adapts to your answers as you go, and the passing standard is 700 on a scale of 0 to 1000.
items: Between 100 and 125 questions, with up to 2 hours to finish. How many you see depends on how the exam goes, as the next sections explain.
Every CC exam, worldwide, uses an adaptive format called Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT). ISC2 has used it for CC since October 1, 2025.
ISC2 lists the question format as multiple choice and advanced item types. It does not show CC examples of the advanced types, so read the instructions on each screen before you answer.
Each exam includes trial questions that do not count toward your score (ISC2 calls them pretest items), 25 in all. They look exactly like the rest, so treat every question as if it counts.
Scores sit on a scale from 0 to 1000, and the passing standard is 700. Your result is reported as a pass or a fail.
Languages: English, Chinese, Japanese, German and Spanish. Chinese is offered only in set windows each year.
ISC2 requires no work experience for CC, so you can sit the exam as a beginner. You must be at least 16 to sit the exam, and candidates aged 16 or 17 must come with a parent or guardian.
The current exam outline took effect on September 1, 2026. It is the first major update since CC launched in August 2022.
KaiSip practice uses four-option multiple choice and does not adapt to you. It builds the thinking the exam tests, but it is not a copy of the real exam.

sections.title: The five domains and their weights
sections.summary: ISC2's outline splits the exam into five domains. A domain's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a good guide to where your study time goes.
items: Security Principles is the largest domain at 24%, about one question in four. It covers the ISC2 Code of Ethics and, new in 2026, due care and due diligence.
Networking and Cloud Security Concepts (21.3%) and Identity and Access Management (20%) come next. With Security Principles, they make up about two thirds of the exam.

Security Governance and Security Operations and Incident Response are 17.3% each. Business continuity and disaster recovery are now covered under redundancy in Governance, and incident response is a major part of Domain 5.
ISC2's table lists a total of 100%, but the five weights as printed add up to 99.9%. Use them as a guide to proportion.
ISC2 places foundational AI topics inside all five domains instead of giving AI a domain of its own. Expect AI in any domain.

sections.title: How the adaptive exam works
sections.summary: In an adaptive exam, the questions you get depend on how you answer earlier ones. The exam stops once it is confident of your result, so its length varies.
items: There is no going back. Once your answer is final, you cannot review or change it, so answer each question carefully before you move on.
After 100 questions, the exam ends as soon as it is 95% confident that your ability is above or below the passing standard. If it is not yet sure, it carries on.
If you reach question 125, or time runs out after you have answered at least 100, you still get a pass or a fail, based on how your answers compare with the passing standard at that point.
Ending at 100 can mean a pass or a fail, and so can going on to 125. The length tells you nothing, so keep your focus on the question in front of you.
Answer at least 100 questions within the 2 hours: at least 75 that count, plus the 25 trial ones. If time runs out before you reach 100, the result is an automatic fail.

sections.title: Read each question as a practitioner
sections.summary: A short routine for every question. These are KaiSip's study patterns, built around ISC2's outline, not rules that ISC2 publishes.
steps: Read the last line first. Find what is being asked: an action, a risk, a purpose or a definition.
Find the priority word (FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST) and keep it in mind while you read the options.
Check your role and the stakes: you are an entry-level practitioner unless told otherwise. Are people at risk? Is this yours to do, or the owner's to decide?
Eliminate two: wrong control type, wrong layer, outside your authority, a skipped procedure or a fix for a symptom.
Decide between the final two: apply the priority word, then prefer the option that keeps people safe, follows the procedure, fits your role and fixes the cause.
Commit and move on. Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice, then confirm. You can't come back to it.
items: People first. When someone's safety is at stake, protecting people comes before data, systems or cost.
Follow policy and procedure. When the procedure gives a task to your role, do it; when it does not, report or escalate to the right owner.
You never accept a risk yourself. The risk owner accepts it within tolerance (the level of risk the organization has agreed it can live with), and senior management decides beyond it.
Pick the basic control that fits the risk, not the biggest or newest one.
Ethics questions draw on the four canons of the ISC2 Code of Ethics. ISC2 gives no rule for ranking the canons, so judge the situation, not the order they are listed in.

sections.title: Pacing your 2 hours
sections.summary: You have up to 2 hours for 100 to 125 questions. You cannot go back, so give each question careful attention once, at a pace that leaves time to spare.
items: 125 questions in 120 minutes is just under a minute each. Aim for about 55 seconds a question so the clock never becomes the problem.
Checkpoints at that pace: question 65 at the 1-hour mark and question 100 near 92 minutes. That leaves time if the exam runs on to 125.
Read the whole question and every option before you confirm. A careful first answer matters more here than on an exam where you can return later.
If a question stalls you past about 90 seconds, rule out what you can, choose your best answer and move on. Running out of time before you reach 100 answers costs far more than one hard question.
You may take breaks, but the clock keeps running: all break time counts toward your 2 hours.
KaiSip's timed mock helps you practice this pace, but it is not adaptive and its score is not an ISC2 score.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You book the exam through your ISC2 account, which sends you on to Pearson VUE to pick a test center and time. The facts below were checked on the date shown; confirm them on isc2.org before you pay.
items: The CC exam costs U.S. $199 in most regions, EUR 191.04 on ISC2's Europe price list and GBP 161.19 in the UK. Taxes depend on where you sit the exam.
An exam bought on its own must be scheduled and taken within 365 days of purchase.

ISC2's free program, One Million Certified in Cybersecurity, closed to new enrollments on May 20, 2026. An unexpired free code must be used to sit the exam by December 31, 2026; an expired code cannot be reactivated. It gives one free attempt only.

Pearson VUE charges U.S. $50 to move a booking and U.S. $100 to cancel, and you cannot move within 24 hours of the appointment. Sitting CC for the first time on a One Million code by December 31, 2026? Moving is free; canceling is not.
Before you pay, also check the ID you must bring and the name it must match, and the deadline to move or cancel without losing the fee.
If you want to sit the exam in Chinese, check ISC2's dates early: it is offered only in set windows each year.
If your book or course is from before September 2026, it follows the older outline. Most topics carry over, but some moved: incident response is now in Domain 5. KaiSip follows the 2026 outline.

sections.title: Where you sit the exam
sections.summary: ISC2 delivers the CC exam only at Pearson VUE test centers: Pearson Professional Centers and ISC2-authorized Pearson Select Test Centers. ISC2 says CC is available only in person; there is no online option.
items: ISC2 does not offer the exam at training events or mobile testing sites. You book a Pearson test center through your ISC2 account, which sends you on to Pearson VUE.
The format is the same at every center: an adaptive exam of 100 to 125 questions in up to 2 hours, with no going back.
If anything in ISC2's or Pearson VUE's instructions is unclear, ask before exam day instead of guessing.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Exam day is about steady attention: answer each question once and carefully, and keep an eye on the clock.
items: Bring the two forms of ID that ISC2 requires, a primary and a secondary, and arrive at least 30 minutes early. Arriving within 15 minutes of your start counts as late and can cost your seat and fee. Check ISC2's rules well before the day.
You cannot review or change an answer once it is final. Read the whole question and every option before you confirm.
Watch your pace. If time runs out before you have answered 100 questions, the result is an automatic fail.
The exam may stop at 100 questions or carry on toward 125. Either is normal, and neither tells you how you did.
Some questions are unscored trial questions, and you can't tell which. If a question feels unfamiliar, it may still count: answer it as well as you can and move on.
You may take breaks, but the clock keeps running: all break time counts toward your 2 hours. You leave the testing room for a break and have a palm vein scan before and after it.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: At check-out, the test center gives you an unofficial pass or fail; ISC2 then emails the official result. Results are sometimes delayed while ISC2 checks its scoring. If you do not pass, you also see how you did by domain.
items: If you do not pass, each domain is ranked as below, near or above the proficiency level. Use that ranking to choose what to study next.
If you need to retake, ISC2 requires a wait of 30 test-free days after your first attempt, 60 after your second, and 90 after your third and any later attempt.
You can attempt the exam at most 4 times in 12 months, and you pay for each retake unless your purchase included a second attempt.
Practice scores in any study app, including KaiSip, are not ISC2 scaled scores and cannot predict your result.
Passing the exam is not the last step. ISC2 decides certification, as the next section explains.

sources.label: ISC2 Insights: what to do after your CC exam (January 2025)

sections.title: Becoming and staying certified
sections.summary: Passing the exam is a big step, but ISC2 decides certification. Following the ISC2 Code of Ethics is a condition of holding it.
items: Following the ISC2 Code of Ethics is a condition of certification. Its four canons are also part of what Domain 1 tests.

The four canons, in ISC2's words: protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession. Principals means your employers and clients.

After you pass, ISC2 emails instructions within about a week. Submit the application within nine months of passing, or you must retake the exam. It includes agreeing to the ISC2 Code of Ethics, and you then pay your first yearly fee of U.S. $50.
To stay certified, earn 45 continuing professional education (CPE) credits in each three-year cycle (ISC2 suggests 15 a year) and pay the U.S. $50 Annual Maintenance Fee (AMF) each year.
